`io_sdram.v` comes from openfpga-core revision `618a3eb`; its Analogue Pocket Framework license is in `sdram-LICENSE`. The controller is designed for 100 MHz and runs at 49.152 MHz in this diagnostic with a 368-clock refresh interval, a chip clock near +243°, and falling-edge DDIO input capture.

`pdc_bridge_cmd.v` derives from the pinned Analogue core template's `core_bridge_cmd.v` under the same framework license. The module is renamed and adds command `0x00B8`: it waits for the video clock domain to confirm the requested grayscale setting before returning the required `0x444D` response. Other host/target commands retain the template implementation.

`psram.sv` comes from pocket-utils revision `78482d1b363606336f4535aa0adc2e957bc20558`; its MIT license is in `psram-LICENSE`. Local changes hold write data for two controller clocks after write enable and chip select are released, use a one-hot cycle marker for pin-control decisions, and prepare address outputs throughout idle independently of request eligibility. The cycle marker preserves the original state intervals and transaction lengths; idle address preparation occurs while both chip selects are inactive. The native wrapper allows 95 ns for read access, 13 ns for chip-select setup and 8 ns for address hold. These counted intervals cover the upstream device requirements plus a 6 ns FPGA pin-delay allowance. The pin-level fixture applies that allowance to control skew and delays device read data by 70 ns plus 6 ns in each direction. TimeQuest validates the asynchronous pin data paths separately at every operating corner.

The Verilator branch models ALTDDIO_IN’s falling-edge register and forwarding latch without adding a second rising-edge flip-flop. This corrects a simulation-only read delay; the synthesized DDIO primitive is unchanged. The pin-level fixture supplies actual CL3 read beats, rather than shortening the memory CAS latency to compensate. See [Altera’s DDR I/O guide](https://www.intel.com/programmable/technical-pdfs/683148.pdf).
